A plan with unlimited data, she pointed out, is rarely needed by someone who lives near a wireless connection.

Aunt Wen made it clear that she was not asking them to give up every want, which would be miserable and, in any case, would not last. Instead, she gave each of them a card and asked them to write down two favourites, things they would genuinely miss. Whatever was on those cards was kept on purpose, and everything else would have to earn its place by becoming a real decision.

Aunt Wen tapped the jar of coins on her counter and then told them the oldest rule she knew, which was to pay yourself first. On the very day wages arrive, before the bills or the shopping, a fixed part is moved into savings and treated as if it did not exist. She had followed this rule since she was nineteen, she said, and she had never once regretted it.

Most people try to save whatever is left at the end of the month, Aunt Wen observed, and what is left is almost always nothing. She compared it to packing tomorrow's lunch before sitting down to dinner, since a lunch that is not packed first will certainly be eaten by the hungry person at the table. Saving first turns the whole habit upside down, and it works for exactly that reason.

Amara worried that saving would mean going without, so Aunt Wen told them to start with an amount so small that they would hardly notice it leaving. They agreed on twenty a week, and Joel, with a flourish, dropped the first coins into a jar on which Ivy had written the word Future in bright felt pen. The sound of the first coins falling to the bottom of the jar was surprisingly satisfying to them both.

Amara could not help thinking aloud that twenty a week seemed hardly worth the effort, and that the sum would not buy much in a year. Aunt Wen only smiled, as though she had heard the objection a hundred times, and explained that at the beginning the habit matters far more than the amount. A tiny habit can be grown, whereas a grand plan that is abandoned by March is worth nothing.

The following morning they visited the bank, where a patient clerk helped them open a second account, which they named Future. It was kept entirely separate from the account they spent from, and that distance was deliberate, because money that is out of sight is far less likely to wander off. Amara signed the form with a slightly trembling hand, as though she were signing a contract with her future self.

On the next payday Joel moved the savings before paying a single bill, and his heart beat a little faster as he pressed the button on his phone. The rent was paid, the food was bought, and the month continued as it always had, except that something small and solid had been set aside. The disaster that he had half expected simply never arrived, and the bills were all paid on time.

Amara bought a stainless steel flask, filled it each morning with coffee brewed in the kitchen, and carried it to the depot in her bag. To her surprise it tasted better than the kiosk's, probably because she knew exactly what it had cost, and it provided most of that first month's savings. The small victory gave her a feeling of quiet competence that she had not felt for a long time.

Ivy's school trip form was finally signed, and the forty was paid out of money that no longer vanished into coffee and snacks. At the school gate Ivy flung her arms around her mother's waist and, wisely, asked no questions at all, although her eyes were very bright. For Amara it was the first proof that the notebook had been worth the trouble.

At the depot Dev noticed that Amara had stopped queuing at the kiosk, and he asked her, in a suspicious tone, whether she had won some money. She drew a jar on a paper napkin and explained the idea of paying yourself first, and he listened with the look of a man who is trying to appear unimpressed. By the end of the break, he had promised, with some reluctance, that he would at least think about it.

After one month, the Future account held eighty, which was hardly a fortune but was eighty more than they had held a month before. Aunt Wen raised her teacup in a small toast and told them that the first eighty are always the hardest, because they prove that it can be done. Joel grinned broadly, and for the first time in years he felt like the true owner of his own money.

Aunt Wen drew a long bar on a sheet of paper and shaded a small part of it, explaining that this was the savings rate. It means simply the share of your income that you keep rather than spend, and it describes the family's habits far better than the size of the pay does. A person who earns a great deal and keeps nothing is poorer in the long run than one who earns less and keeps a steady part.

Joel took the calculator and divided their monthly savings of eighty by the whole of their pay, and the answer was disappointingly small. It came to less than two percent, a start, as Aunt Wen cheerfully admitted, but a very modest one. She reminded him that a seed is also very small on the day it is planted.

Aunt Wen then wrote down a goal that many financial writers suggest, which is to keep about a tenth of income and to rise higher when life allows. She stressed that this was a rule of thumb and not a law, because a young family with small children and a grandparent in the same house might need a different figure altogether. What mattered most was to know the number, to say it aloud, and to watch it slowly move.

That evening Amara sat on the sofa with her phone and scrolled through the list of regular payments that left the account each month. To her dismay, several of them were for services that nobody in the family could remember choosing, and a few had been running for years. It was like finding unlabelled keys on a ring and realising that each one opened a door she no longer used.

At the back of a kitchen drawer, beneath a tangle of old batteries and takeaway menus, Joel found his gym card, which was slightly bent. The gym had been taking thirty a month for half a year, and he had not set foot inside it since a brief burst of enthusiasm in the spring. He felt as though he had been paying a stranger to be healthy on his behalf.

A free trial that the family had started during the winter had quietly turned into a paid service, and the money had been leaving ever since. Nobody had noted the date on which the trial ended, and the company had, quite naturally, hoped that nobody would. It was a reminder that many of the world's small leaks are designed to be forgotten.

Amara spent the better part of an evening on the telephone, working steadily through her list and cancelling the services that nobody used. Each call demanded some patience, and one polite young man even tried to tempt her with a discount, but she held firm. Every payment she cancelled gave a small amount of money back to the family, month after month, without any further effort.

The family gathered on the sofa and voted, with raised hands, on which service deserved to survive, and the winner was the one that everybody actually watched. Ivy campaigned fiercely for her game pass, but when her mother asked how often she had played it, she admitted, with some embarrassment, that it was twice. The vote was cheerful and good-humoured, and nobody in the room felt that they were being punished.

Amara set a reminder on her phone for a few days before every renewal date, so that no payment could ever creep up on them unnoticed again. The purpose was not to cancel everything but to make each renewal a conscious choice, so that the family paid only for what it valued. A calendar, she discovered with some surprise, can be every bit as useful as a strong lock.

The cancelled payments freed sixty-seven a month, and Joel moved the whole amount straight into the Future account before it could be spent on anything else. Their savings rate rose to about three percent, which was still small beside the tenth that Aunt Wen had described, but it was moving in the right direction. Amara said the climb felt like walking uphill with the wind finally behind her.

Aunt Wen took the calculator and showed them what their daily coffee cost over a longer span of time. A cup of four, bought on twenty-two working days, came to eighty-eight a month, and over a full year the sum rose above a thousand. It was the same story as the dripping tap, only this time the water was being poured into a paper cup.

Aunt Wen did not tell Amara to give up coffee, since she believed that a life without small pleasures is a life that quickly collapses. She asked only one question, which was whether each cup truly brought joy or whether it was simply a habit with a lid on. Amara thought honestly about it and decided to keep a single coffee out each Friday, and to make the rest at home.

Joel looked hard at his garage snacks and decided that most of them were bought out of boredom rather than hunger, since he was surrounded by good bread all night. He began to pack a lunchbox with fresh loaves, cheese and an apple, and he allowed himself one treat a week. He found, to his surprise, that a treat tastes much better when it is rare.

Aunt Wen then introduced a tool that she called price per use, which is the cost of an object divided by the number of times that it is used. It shows what is truly cheap, and the answer is often very different from what the price tag suggests at first glance. A low price on something that sits in a cupboard is, in the end, a high price.

Joel remembered his old boots, which had cost thirty and fallen apart after fifteen wears, a price of two for every wear. A good pair at one hundred and twenty, worn a hundred and twenty times, would cost only one for each wear, which made the expensive boots the cheaper choice in the long run. He shook his head at the thought of all the cheap bargains he had bought and thrown away.

Then Joel confessed to the fancy blender that sat on a high shelf with a film of dust upon its lid, bought after a persuasive advertisement. It had been used twice and had cost sixty, so each use had cost thirty, while the humble kettle in the kitchen, boiled every day for years, cost almost nothing per use. The comparison made them both laugh out loud, and Joel promised to sell the blender to someone who would use it.

For anything that was not a genuine need, Aunt Wen recommended a rule so simple that it seemed almost silly: wait two days before buying it. The next afternoon Amara stood in a clothes shop with a jacket in her hands, felt the old excitement rising, and put it quietly back on the shelf. She walked out into the busy street feeling much lighter and, oddly enough, a little triumphant, like someone who has won a small battle.

They added a page to the notebook titled Wait List, on which every wanted item was written with the date it was first desired. After two days they looked at the list again and asked, in cold blood, whether they still wanted each thing. The method was dull and almost insultingly easy, and it worked better than any amount of willpower.

At the end of the month, they went through the wait list together, and seven items had been written down in all. Only two of them were still wanted with any real feeling, and the other five had faded from their minds like mist on a morning bus window. The money they had not spent on those five, Amara pointed out, was quietly sitting in the Future account.

A large sign above a crowded shelf announced that everything was half price, and Joel felt the old tug in his chest, as strong as a magnet. Then he heard Aunt Wen's calm voice in his head, saying that a bargain you do not need is still money spent, and that the only truly cheap thing is the thing you never buy. He put the basket back on the floor by the door and walked out into the sunshine feeling like a man who had been set free.

One bright Saturday the neighbours, Tomas and Lina, rolled a gleaming new car into their driveway, and its paint shone like a polished spoon. Joel watched from the kitchen window with his tea going cold and felt a sharp pang of envy, which he found surprising and rather unpleasant. For a moment, the old car in front of his own house looked tired and embarrassing.

When Joel described the new car to Aunt Wen, she lifted one eyebrow and observed that you cannot see what another person owes. A glossy car on a driveway may have been bought with years of savings, but it may equally have been bought entirely on debt, and the paint looks identical in both cases. Other people's possessions, she said, are therefore never a reliable picture of their true finances at home.

Later that week Lina sat beside Amara on a doorstep, holding a mug of tea and a crumpled letter from the finance company, and confessed that the car payments were keeping her awake. Tomas had taken extra shifts to keep up with the cost, and the children rarely saw him before bedtime. It was a hard thing to hear, and Amara left feeling grateful for her own plain, paid-for little car.

On his lunch break Joel wandered onto a car dealer's forecourt, telling himself that he was only looking, and a smiling salesman appeared at his elbow within seconds. The man talked at length about the small monthly payment, the generous trade-in and the wonderful smell of the leather, but he never once mentioned the total price. It was a clever way to make something large seem small, and Joel recognised the trick from the notebook.

Standing between a brand new car and a three-year-old one of the same model, Joel recalled what Aunt Wen had taught him about value. A new car loses a large share of its worth in its first few years, which means that the first owner pays for the loss while the second owner collects the bargain. A good used car could therefore give him nearly the same comfort for a good deal less money.

Joel drove his old car to Ade, a mechanic who had known the family for years and who judged cars the way a doctor judges patients, with a calm squint. After half an hour under the bonnet, Ade wiped his hands and declared that the engine was sound and that, with regular servicing, it had years left. The bill for the check was small, and Joel drove home feeling as though he had been given a pardon.

That Friday Rosa called Joel into her cramped office, which smelled of flour and cinnamon, and thanked him for his loyalty with a pay rise. After tax it came to one hundred and sixty extra each month, and Joel ran the whole way home to tell Amara, who was surprised to find tears in her own eyes. Under the joy, though, a small worry stirred about where all that extra money might quietly disappear to.

Aunt Wen drew a staircase on a sheet of paper and wrote the word spending on every step, each one a little higher than the last, as pay climbed alongside. She called this lifestyle creep, the tendency of spending to rise quietly with income until a bigger wage no longer feels like any more than the old one. It is a trap, she said, that catches the careless and the clever alike.

Amara took a pen, drew a line through the middle of the pay rise, and suggested that they save one half and enjoy the other half without any guilt. Joel agreed at once, and that Friday the whole family ate pizza in a proper restaurant, where Noah blew bubbles into his lemonade and Ivy ordered dessert first. The pleasure was real, and so was the eighty that went into the Future account.

Joel found an empty jam jar, painted the words Car Fund on its side, and set it carefully beside the car keys in the hall. The idea was to save a little each month, so that when the old car finally gave up, a good used one could be bought with cash rather than a loan. He felt, strangely, as proud of the jar as another man might have been of a sports car.

Amara drew a circle on a sheet of paper to stand for their whole income and shaded a very large slice to represent their home. Housing is usually the biggest single cost in a family's life, Aunt Wen explained, and a common rule of thumb keeps it under about a third of income. The rule is not a law, but it is a useful warning light on the dashboard.

In the depot canteen Dev showed Amara a letter from his landlord, and the figure on it took a great deal more than a third of his pay. He looked tired and bewildered as he asked what a person could possibly do about rent, which could not be cut like a coffee habit. Amara promised to ask Aunt Wen, and she suspected that there would be no easy answer.

At the kitchen table Amara read through her rental agreement with a pen in her hand and discovered that the rent would rise at the end of the year. Rather than panic, she wrote a polite note to the landlord, asking whether the rent could stay the same if the family promised to remain for another two years. Aunt Wen warned her that the answer might be no, but that asking is always free.

Joel stopped wandering into the supermarket without a plan, and instead sat down on Sunday evening to write a list of meals for the week. He checked what was already in the fridge before writing a single item, and then he bought only the things that were missing. The old method of filling a basket on impulse now seemed as foolish as carrying water in a sieve.

One evening the family emptied the kitchen bin onto old newspaper and inspected the contents with grim curiosity: wilted vegetables, a stale half loaf, and the remains of a tub of yoghurt. Added up over a week, the wasted food came to about twenty, which meant more than eighty a month was going straight into the rubbish. It was a leak that had, until now, smelled bad but had never been counted.

On Sundays Ivy stirred a large pot of soup while Noah, with great seriousness, wrote the date on labels for the freezer boxes in uneven capital letters. The idea was to cook once and eat twice, so that a tired Wednesday night would hold no temptation to order a takeaway. The kitchen filled with the smell of onions, and the family sat down to a meal that cost very little and tasted wonderful.

Amara learned to ignore the large price printed on the pack and to read the smaller price per kilo on the shelf label, which allowed her to compare unlike things fairly. Sometimes the large pack turned out to be the better buy, but sometimes the tidy little box was cheaper, and the label told her which was which. It felt like learning to read a language that the shops had always hoped she would not understand.

An energy bill arrived one morning, and Aunt Wen, who was visiting, suggested a handful of easy changes that required no sacrifice at all. Switching off lamps in empty rooms, closing windows when the heating was on and washing clothes at a lower temperature would each save a little, and together they would save a good deal. She called this the quietest kind of income, because it arrived without anyone having to work a single extra hour.

Joel bought a strip of foam for a few coins and fitted it along the bottom of the draughty front door, and the cold air that used to creep across the hall stopped as though it had been told off. Noah was appointed the official light inspector and patrolled the flat each evening with a torch, solemnly switching off every lamp left in an empty room. The family laughed about it, but the bill, a month later, was noticeably smaller.

Once a year, Aunt Wen advised, it is worth comparing the price of energy, phone and internet plans, since companies often reward new customers while quietly raising prices for loyal ones. Amara spent a Saturday morning with the laptop, switched two of the plans, and was pleased to find that the family now saved about one hundred and ten each month. It was not hard, she reflected, to think of a good use for that money, and the notebook already suggested one.

A credit card statement dropped onto the kitchen table one morning with a large interest figure printed in the corner, and Joel slid it face down beneath the fruit bowl. Aunt Wen, who was there for tea, retrieved it gently and observed that debt carrying a high rate of interest works against you every hour of every day, even while you sleep. They must therefore begin, she said, by listing every debt and the rate it carried.

Aunt Wen explained that interest is simply the price of borrowing money, and she wrote a sum on her notepad to show how heavy it can be. If two thousand is owed at twenty-four percent a year, she said, the interest alone costs about forty each month, which is money paid for nothing at all. It was a startling idea that a person could work hard all month simply to feed a number on a page.

Joel took a plain card and copied the debts onto it, one to a line, with the amount owed and the interest rate beside each. There was a credit card of two thousand at twenty-four percent, a smaller card of six hundred at eighteen, and the sofa loan of nine hundred at a gentler ten. Seeing them together was frightening for a moment, and then, strangely, a relief, because a known enemy is easier to fight.

Aunt Wen was firm about one rule above all the others, which was that they must pay at least the minimum on every debt, and always on the due date. A late payment brings fees, and a poor record of repayments can make future borrowing harder and more expensive, so a missed date costs far more than the money it seems to save. Amara circled every due date on the kitchen calendar in thick blue pen, so that none of them could be forgotten.

With a pencil, Aunt Wen sketched two paths on a map that led to the same destination, one steep and direct, the other gentle and winding. Paying the highest interest first saves the most money in the end, she said, while paying the smallest debt first feels quicker because debts vanish sooner, and either path will work as long as you keep walking. The only real mistake, she added with a smile, is to stand still at the crossroads and do nothing at all.

Amara and Joel talked it over for an evening and then voted, and the decision was to attack the card with the highest rate first, since it was the one costing them most. Joel asked, half joking and half serious, whether they could celebrate every milestone, and Amara agreed at once, knowing that a plan which brings a little joy is a plan that survives. They shook hands across the table like two business partners who had just signed an important contract.

Each month the money freed by their earlier changes, the cancelled payments, the food that was no longer wasted and the cheaper bills, flowed towards the big card, and the total came to about three hundred. Amara set the payment up on her phone for the day after wages arrived, and she watched with quiet delight as the interest figure on the statement began, month by month, to shrink. It was the first time that the numbers had ever seemed to be working for them.

Joel drew a tall thermometer on the fridge door in red pen and coloured it in from the bottom each time the balance fell, so that the family could see their progress at a glance. Noah checked it every morning before breakfast, announcing the new height in a solemn voice and declaring that it looked like a rocket preparing for take-off. The kitchen had, in its own modest way, become a small launch site for a much larger journey.

Amara slid the credit card into the back of a kitchen drawer and decided to use her debit card for everyday spending, which left her with less temptation and a clearer mind. She also made herself a rule that if a card were ever used again, it would be paid off in full at the end of the month, so that on most cards no interest would be charged at all. Paid in full and on time, a card can be a useful tool, whereas left unpaid month after month, it quickly becomes a trap.

After two months, the big balance had fallen from two thousand to about fourteen hundred, and the red line on the thermometer had climbed past the first mark. Rosa, who had heard about the project from Joel, baked a small cake with a candle on top, and the family ate it standing around the fridge like people at a very strange party. Noah blew out the candle with enormous enthusiasm, and Joel made a silent wish that the red line would keep rising.

One Tuesday the washing machine shuddered, gave a long groan and stopped in the middle of a wash, leaving a grey puddle spreading across the kitchen floor. The repair man arrived promptly and left with one hundred and fifty, and because the family had no savings to draw upon, the bill went straight onto the credit card. Joel stared at the receipt and understood, with a sinking heart, how easily a small accident can undo months of effort.

Aunt Wen listened to the story with a grave expression and then remarked that this was precisely why people keep an emergency cushion. It is a sum of money set aside for surprises and nothing else, so that a broken machine, a sudden medical bill or a lost job does not turn into fresh debt. A cushion cannot prevent trouble, she said, but it can certainly soften the fall for everyone who lands on it.

On the back of an envelope Aunt Wen drew a staircase with three steps and wrote a goal on each. The first was a modest starter of about one thousand, which would cover most small shocks, the second was a full month of essential costs, and the third was the long climb towards three to six months of costs. Nobody, she said gently, has ever built a staircase by jumping straight to the top, so they should start on the first step.

That evening Amara listed their essential costs on a clean page: rent, food, heating, transport, the phone, school costs and insurance. The total came to about two thousand eight hundred a month, which would be the target of the second step, and the figure seemed both enormous and, once written down, reassuringly definite. It is, as Amara remarked to Joel, much easier to climb towards a clear number than towards a thick and frightening fog.

Amara opened a new account at the bank and named it Safety, and she moved the eight hundred that had gathered in the Future account into it as the seed of the cushion. The account was kept separate from everyday spending, so that it would not be raided on a whim, but it was easy to reach, so that it could be used within a day when a real crisis arrived. Its purpose was security, and its reward, as Amara soon discovered, was a deeper and calmer kind of sleep at night.

One day Joel saw a large television at a reduced price and announced, with a grin, that it was an emergency, but Amara calmly held up three fingers. Aunt Wen's test, she reminded him, had three questions: was the expense a surprise, was it truly needed, and was it urgent? A sale on something that you did not plan to buy is a tempting offer, but it is never, under any circumstances, an emergency.

There was a problem that Aunt Wen was frank about, which was that no family can build a cushion and clear a card with the same coin, so each goal had to be given its fair share. After talking it through, they decided to send most of the free money to the credit card, because its interest was so high, and a smaller portion to Safety every month. It was a compromise, certainly, but it was a sensible compromise that kept both goals alive and moving forward together.

Aunt Wen then explained that basic insurance is a cushion's partner, since it protects savings from the largest shocks, such as a car accident, a house fire or a flood. She advised them to find out exactly what each policy covered, to compare prices from time to time, and to buy only the protection that matched a genuine risk. The aim, she said with a smile, was a sturdy fence around the house, and certainly not a fortress with a moat.

Amara spent an evening at the kitchen table with a ruler beneath each line of the insurance papers, reading the small print that most people never read. She compared three offers, noticed that two of them left out something important, and eventually found cover that was just as good as the old one but cost fifteen a month less. She was astonished that an hour of attention could be worth so much money.

A few weeks later Ade telephoned to say that the old car needed a new part, and the whole bill would come to two hundred and twenty. This time the Safety account paid, and not a single coin went onto a credit card, so Joel drove away smiling and told Amara that he felt like a king. Together they began at once to refill the account, because a cushion is only useful if it is ready for the next surprise.

Aunt Wen set two jars side by side on her counter, one labelled Summer Trip and the other New Bed, and invited Amara and Joel to study them. A jar with a name, she said, feels far more real than a pile of money with no particular purpose, and a goal that can be seen is a goal that is much harder to forget. People, she added with a twinkle, are always very bad at saving for nothing in particular, but surprisingly good at saving for something.

At the kitchen table Amara and Joel wrote their goals on three paper labels and stuck them proudly onto the jars. They chose Safety, Car Fund and a Summer Trip to the sea, and Noah decorated the last label with blue waves and a very large yellow sun that took up most of the space. For the first time, their savings had names and faces rather than a single anonymous balance.

Aunt Wen unrolled an old calendar with certain months circled where she had known that heavy bills would fall, and she explained the idea of a sinking fund. A known yearly cost is divided by twelve and put aside a little at a time, so that when the bill finally arrives, the money has been quietly waiting. It is a way of turning a nasty surprise into a gentle, predictable routine.

Amara sat down with the previous year's papers and listed everything that came only once a year: the car service, school clothes and supplies, birthday and festival gifts, and visits to the dentist. The total came to one thousand four hundred and forty, which, when divided by twelve, gave a monthly figure of exactly one hundred and twenty. It was a large sum, but when it was spread across twelve months it looked perfectly manageable and almost friendly.

Joel opened a small account at the bank, named it Yearly Bills, and scheduled a monthly move of one hundred and twenty from the main account on the day after wages. The money would sit quietly there, doing nothing but waiting, like a patient guest at a station who knows that the right train will arrive eventually. He felt oddly organised and grown-up, which was a new and rather pleasant feeling for a man who had once lost a whole month's wages.

When the school's uniform bill arrived, Amara read it at the kitchen table, took a sip of tea and paid it from her phone in half a minute. Before the new system it would have caused a week of worry and an argument, but now the money was already waiting for it, and nothing in the house shook at all. She realised that calm, too, can be bought in advance, and that, in the end, it costs a great deal less than panic.

Amara and Joel danced in the kitchen one evening beside a small jar labelled Fun, with the radio playing and the children laughing in the doorway. Aunt Wen had warned them that a budget with no room for pleasure is a budget that will break, because people cannot live on discipline alone. They therefore set aside a modest sum each month to be enjoyed without a trace of guilt.

Joel loved his video games, and Amara loved her Friday coffees and the occasional new scarf, and neither wished to explain these tastes to the other. They therefore agreed that each of them would receive fifty a month of personal fun money, to be spent on anything at all, and that nobody would ask any questions. It was a small rule, but it quietly removed an enormous number of small quarrels that had been spoiling their evenings for years.

On Saturday they spent part of their fun money on a night at the cinema with a large bowl of buttery popcorn, and they enjoyed every minute of it. The film was not especially good, but that hardly mattered, because the money had been planned for precisely this purpose and there was no guilty voice whispering in the dark. Amara reflected, as the credits rolled, that joy bought on purpose is quite possibly the best and most lasting kind of all.

On the twentieth of the month, Joel opened his fun jar and found that it was empty, and he scowled at it for a minute with real irritation. Then, remembering that the rule was a rule, he decided to wait for the first of the month, and he discovered that waiting was not as terrible as he had imagined. The jar, he understood at last, was a fence that kept his spending safely inside a line, and certainly not a hole in his pocket.

Amara drew a circle on a fresh page with the help of a ruler and divided it into three sections for needs, wants and saving. Their needs took up about fifty-eight percent of their pay, the wants about twenty-two percent, and the rest, about a fifth, went to saving and paying off debts. A simple split of this kind gives a family a starting picture, and the picture can always be adjusted as life changes.

A few days later the landlord replied to Amara's polite note and agreed to a smaller rise, though not to no rise at all. Amara cheerfully redrew her circle with the new rent, shaving a little from the wants and adding a little to the needs, since a plan that cannot bend will certainly break when the first storm arrives. Aunt Wen nodded approvingly and said that flexibility was the secret ingredient of every lasting budget.

One quiet evening Amara and Joel sat side by side on the sofa with the notebook open between them and talked about their money, calmly and without raised voices. They agreed that the point was to work as a team against a common problem, and that nobody was going to blame anybody else for past mistakes. It felt strange to speak so openly, and also like putting down something very heavy that both of them had been carrying alone.

Once a month they held a money date, with a pot of tea on the table and their phones turned face down so that nothing could interrupt them. Each of them shared one win, one worry and one decision, which kept the conversation honest and short, and the meeting seldom lasted longer than half an hour. They discovered that the less often the topic was avoided, the less frightening it became.

One evening Joel looked at his hands and admitted, in a low voice, that his parents had never spoken about money when he was a boy, so he had learned to look away from it whenever it appeared. Amara put her hand over his and said that looking at it together was the whole idea of the evening, and that she had not been much braver herself. They sat for a while in a comfortable silence, as people do when a weight has been shared.

Aunt Wen observed that children learn far more from what they see their parents do than from anything they are told, and that they are watching more closely than most adults imagine. The best lesson she knew was to give a child small amounts of money that were truly their own, to save, to spend and to share. Mistakes made with a few coins are cheap, she said, while mistakes made later with a salary are not.

Ivy, who was ten and rather proud of her new responsibility, received six a week in pocket money and labelled three small jars: Save, Spend and Share. Each Saturday morning she divided the coins with great ceremony, three into the first jar, two into the second and one into the third, and she counted them twice to be certain. Her father observed that she had a better system than most grown-ups he knew.

Noah, who was seven and impatient, spent his own coins on a cheap plastic toy that caught his eye in a shop window, and it broke within two days. He was inconsolable for an hour, but the lesson sank in more deeply than any lecture could have done, which was that coins do not simply grow back and that cheap things are often the most expensive. The next time he wanted a toy, he asked, with a very serious face, whether he could wait a few days first.

Ivy had set her heart on a second-hand bicycle that she had seen at a street market for sixty, and she began to save for it a little every week. When she finally had the money, she compared the price against three other bicycles, and her father crouched beside her to test the brakes and to squeeze the tyres. She wheeled it home through the busy streets with an expression of fierce, quiet pride that stayed on her face all evening.

Once a month, after the money date, the whole family gathered around the table with a notebook and a plate of cake for what they called the family meeting. Each person, even Noah, was entitled to a say in one small thing, such as where they would go on Sunday or which film they would watch together. The children soon learned that a vote counts for much more when the money behind it has been planned.

One afternoon Amara noticed a poster for evening classes pinned to the depot wall beside the bus timetable, and she stopped to read it twice. Aunt Wen had taught her that there are three ways to raise the savings rate: to spend less, to earn more, or to do both together. Earning more, whether through a new skill, a better job or a small side income, was a door that she had not yet tried.

Aunt Wen drew a floor and a ceiling on a sheet of paper and explained that spending can only be cut as far as the floor, which is zero, while earning has no ceiling at all. A sensible plan, she said, uses both, since a family that only cuts costs will eventually run out of things to cut. It was an encouraging thought, because it meant that effort could always be turned into progress.

The depot offered a course for driver trainers, and after the company had paid half, the fee came to one hundred and twenty. Amara weighed it exactly as she would weigh any purchase, asking what it would cost per use, and the answer was that the course could pay for itself within a few months if it led to a better role. For once, spending a little money seemed to be the wisest possible way of saving a great deal more of it.

Joel had been thinking for weeks about a small idea, and one morning he finally asked Rosa whether he might bake loaves on Saturday afternoons to sell at a market stall. She laughed, wiped her floury hands on her apron, and agreed, as long as he paid a small fee for the use of her oven and her flour. His heart leapt with excitement, and he walked home through the dawn composing new recipes in his head.

Joel learned from Aunt Wen that profit is not the money taken in, but what remains after every cost has been subtracted from it. He therefore counted the flour, the yeast, the paper bags, the oven fee and the stall fee, and, most importantly, a fair price for his own tired hours. At the end of his first market day, the sum was small but real, and every coin of it was his.

Amara studied late into the night at the kitchen table, with the textbook propped against the fruit bowl, while Joel brought her tea and tiptoed around the sleeping flat. The family shared the chores without being asked, and Ivy took charge of the dishes in a very businesslike way. Aunt Wen, however, insisted that Amara also protect her rest, since a tired mind makes poor decisions.

When the results arrived, Amara had passed with high marks, and Dev clapped so loudly in the depot canteen that the cook looked out of the kitchen in alarm. A few days later the company offered her the post of driver trainer, with a pay rise of two hundred a month after tax, and she accepted before the manager had finished the sentence. She went home that evening feeling several inches taller than she had that morning.

The new pay was divided in the same way as Joel's raise had been, half to savings and half to enjoyment, and nobody found it difficult to agree. Joel opened a second page in the notebook for the money from his stall, and they decided that all of it would be saved, since they had never counted on it and would not miss it. The family was learning that extra income, like a new habit, vanishes quickly unless it is given a job to do the moment it arrives.

Aunt Wen tapped a tax form on her kitchen table and reminded them that extra income may be taxed, and that the rules differ from one country to another. She could not say what applied where they lived, and neither could anyone else without checking, so Amara and Joel visited the website of the tax office and read it carefully. A little time spent on rules, Aunt Wen told them, is cheaper than a large surprise.

One evening the family stood in front of the chart on the fridge and saw that the line had finally climbed past a quarter. Saving and debt payments together now took about a quarter of their pay, and nothing that mattered had been lost, which was the most surprising part of all. They had given up very little, and they had gained a great deal of calm.

At the end of the month Amara opened the bank statement and noticed a short new line labelled interest, sitting quietly beside the Safety balance. It was only a few coins, but it was money that the account had earned entirely by itself, without a single extra hour of work from either of them. She stared at it for some time, as one might stare at the first flower of spring.

Aunt Wen drew a bank on her notepad with arrows pointing in and out, and she explained that a bank lends out many of the deposits that it receives. The interest that it pays to savers is a share of what it earns from lending, which is why the bank is willing to pay anything at all for the use of your money. It is, she said, a sensible arrangement for both sides, as long as the saver is not careless.

On the laptop Amara set two savings accounts side by side and compared the rates, and Aunt Wen showed her what the difference meant in real money. On three thousand, an interest rate of one percent pays thirty in a year, while four percent pays one hundred and twenty, so a small difference in the rate becomes a large difference in the reward. The figures were only an imagined illustration, she warned, but the lesson behind them was perfectly solid and well worth remembering.

Joel read the small print of the account with the patience of a man who had once been caught by a trial offer, and he found that the rules about taking money out varied widely. Some accounts allowed withdrawals at any time, while others locked the money away for a fixed term, which was perfectly reasonable for a long goal but useless for an emergency cushion. The right account, he decided, depended entirely on the job it was hired to do.

Aunt Wen added a careful warning, which was that many countries protect the money in bank accounts up to a stated limit if the bank should ever fail. The rules differ from place to place, and some protect more than others, so it is worth checking exactly how your bank is covered before you place a large sum with it. She said that this was a matter of reading, not of fear, and that it took ten minutes.

That Saturday Amara moved the Safety fund to a better account that still allowed instant access, which took twenty minutes on her phone and a good deal of squinting. The following month a slightly larger line of interest appeared on the statement, and she felt the quiet satisfaction of a person who has found a leak and sealed it. It was the first time in her life that her money had ever worked quietly through the night while she slept.

Aunt Wen set a shopping basket on the table, filled it with oranges, bread and tea, and then, as she raised a price tag on each item, removed one thing at a time. This, she said, is inflation, the slow rise in prices over time, which means that money kept as plain cash buys a little less with every passing year. It does not shout, but like a rising tide it moves steadily in only one direction.

From a drawer in her old desk Aunt Wen took a faded price tag from her very first year in the shop and laid it beside a modern one. A loaf of bread that had cost one in those days now cost three, and the same coin, she noted, bought far less than it had once done. It was a vivid reminder that the value of money is not fixed but is always quietly moving.

Aunt Wen offered an imagined example, saying that it was an illustration and not a forecast, in which prices rose by three percent every year. After ten years, what one hundred buys today would cost about one hundred and thirty-five, so one hundred left under a mattress would be able to buy only about three quarters of the same goods. The difference, she said with a gentle shrug, is simply the hidden price of doing nothing at all with your money.

Joel drew two lines on a sheet of squared paper, one for the interest that a savings account might pay and one for the rise in prices, and the lines ran close together. A good savings account, Aunt Wen agreed, may do little more than keep pace with rising prices, and that is exactly what a cushion needs to do. For goals that lie many years ahead, however, cash alone may not be enough.

Aunt Wen set a small potted plant next to the pile of coins on her counter and explained that goals which lie many years ahead call for a different tool. Many people use low-cost investments for such goals, because over long periods they have often grown faster than prices have risen, although they carry risks that a bank account does not. She was careful to add that she was explaining ideas and not recommending any particular product.

Aunt Wen drew two boxes on her notepad, one labelled Saving and the other Investing, and explained the difference with great care. Investing means owning a small share of something, such as a company, a property or a collection of both, and the value of that share can rise or fall from one year to the next. There is no promise, she said, and anyone who offers one is not to be trusted.

On the kitchen calendar, Aunt Wen circled a period of five years and observed that money needed sooner than this should not be placed in investments that can fall. That was the reason, she said, that the Safety fund and the Yearly Bills account would remain in the bank, where the money was easy to reach and did not change in value. Only money that could wait for a long time was a candidate for anything else.

Aunt Wen filled a bowl with apples, oranges, pears and plums, then held up a single apple beside it and asked which was the safer meal. A fund, she explained, holds a small piece of a great many companies at once, so that if one of them fails the damage is shared among all the rest. This is called spreading the risk, and it is one of the few sensible protections an ordinary saver has.

From a plant on her windowsill Aunt Wen hung two paper price tags, one large and one tiny, and explained that yearly fees quietly reduce what an investor keeps. A charge that looks small, such as two percent a year, can swallow a very large share of the growth over several decades, whereas a fund with a tiny charge leaves far more of it to the saver. It is a curious fact, she added, that most investors never read the line that states the fee at all.

Aunt Wen then described what she called the slow miracle of compounding: the earnings of money can earn further earnings of their own, so that growth builds upon growth like the branches of a tree. In an imagined example, a thousand invested at five percent a year grows to about sixteen hundred and thirty in ten years and about two thousand six hundred and fifty in twenty. The longer the money is left alone, she pointed out, the steeper and the more spectacular the curve of growth becomes.

Joel worked through an imagined example on the calculator while Amara watched over his shoulder: one hundred put aside every month for twenty years, earning five percent a year. The total came to about forty-one thousand, even though only twenty-four thousand had been paid in, and the difference was the work done by compounding. Aunt Wen reminded them firmly that this was an illustration and not a promise.

Aunt Wen sketched two saplings on a sheet of paper, one planted today and one planted a decade later, each nourished by the same one hundred a month. If the saving began ten years later, the second sapling would reach only about fifteen and a half thousand, which is less than half of what its older sister would become. The lesson, she said, is that time is a priceless ingredient, quite as valuable as money itself.

One evening a newspaper headline announced that investment prices had fallen for several months in a row, and Amara felt a cold wave of nervousness in her chest. Aunt Wen, who had lived through several such periods, said calmly that markets rise and fall and that patience usually beats panic, though she admitted that nothing in this field is guaranteed. A person who cannot sleep because of the risk, she added, is taking too much of it.

That night Amara drew a staircase of goals on a large sheet of paper and marked the first step clearly in blue. After talking it through, they decided to clear the big credit card before they began to invest, because paying off a debt that charged twenty-four percent was as good as a safe gain of the same size. Investing, Aunt Wen agreed with an approving nod, would be a later step on the staircase and certainly not the first.

Joel and Amara sat at the kitchen table one evening and, with a few taps on the phone, scheduled a monthly transfer to happen on the day after wages arrived. From then on saving was done first and without any effort, and spending became the activity that required a choice, which was exactly the reverse of how it had been before. It was the neatest trick in the whole plan, and it needed no willpower at all.

On the laptop screen a tidy list of scheduled moves glowed in a column, each with its own name and its own date. Every payday, money travelled quietly and without fuss to Safety, to Yearly Bills, to the Car Fund and the Summer Trip, and a large portion went to the credit card as well. Amara thought of it as a small and very obedient river, flowing exactly where she had told it to go.

Joel frowned at the list, because he could not shake the feeling that the money was now running without him, and he did not entirely like it. Aunt Wen tapped the table and said that the control had not vanished but had simply moved to the moment when the plan was set up, and to the monthly check that followed it. A pilot, she remarked, does not hold the aircraft by hand for the whole journey, but he does watch the instruments.

In the festival month, the family travelled to visit relatives, bought gifts for everyone, ate out far too often and forgot, for a while, to write anything in the notebook. By the thirty-first, the page was full of red numbers, and both Amara and Joel felt the old shame creeping back like a damp patch on a wall. It looked, for a moment, as though all their hard work had melted away.

Aunt Wen opened her old green ledger at a page covered in crossings-out and told them that this had been the worst year of her life with money, thirty years earlier. She had overspent, lost heart and nearly stopped keeping the book at all, but she had started again the following month and had never regretted it. One bad month, or even one bad year, she said, should never be allowed to end a plan.

Amara took the notebook, turned to a clean page and wrote three short lines: what happened, what to try differently, and the date to begin again. They agreed that the date would be the first of the month, and when it arrived, it felt like turning over a fresh page in a book that they were happy to keep reading. The shame, they found, evaporated surprisingly fast once there was a plan in front of it.

Aunt Wen told them that windfalls such as bonuses, gifts and refunds are the true test of a plan, because they arrive without effort and are therefore easy to waste. A sensible rule, she suggested, is to split the money at once, with a small part for pleasure and the larger part for the goals that matter. That way, she said, a lucky day brings both a small celebration and some real progress towards the goals.

Rosa handed Joel an envelope marked Thank You on the last morning before the holiday, and inside it was a bonus of two hundred, which was far more than he had expected. After a short family discussion, they kept fifty for a treat, a Sunday outing to the seaside with ice cream, and sent the remaining hundred and fifty directly to the big credit card. The red thermometer on the fridge door climbed another satisfying inch, and Noah cheered as he coloured it in.

Amara had acquired a new habit of reading each bill with a pencil in her hand, and one evening she circled a line on the energy bill that simply did not look right. A telephone call confirmed that the company had charged her twice for the same period, and a week later they sent back ninety with a polite apology. It was, she told Joel, the best pay she had ever earned for ten minutes of reading.

One morning at the depot Dev stepped down from his bus, held up his phone and showed Amara the first balance in his new savings account, with the pride of a boy displaying a fish. He had set up an automatic transfer on payday, he said, and he no longer had to remember anything, and his grin was as wide as the windscreen of his bus. Amara congratulated him warmly, and secretly she felt almost as proud as he did.

A message arrived on Amara's phone one lunchtime promising enormous profits within a few days, and it was written in the breathless style of an advertisement for a miracle. She read it with mounting suspicion and then shook her head and deleted it, remembering that offers of quick and certain riches are among the oldest warning signs there are. Aunt Wen had added a second rule, which was that nobody, for any reason, should share a password or a code.

One evening in the supermarket car park, a man in a shiny jacket handed Joel a glossy leaflet and told him, in a confidential whisper, that he could double his money in a single month. Joel felt the tug of the offer immediately, because the Car Fund was growing so slowly, and the leaflet made the words sound like a gift. He took it home and put it on the table, where it seemed to glow.

Aunt Wen examined the leaflet as a doctor might examine a sample, and then she counted five warning signs on her fingers. They were a promise of guaranteed profit, pressure to act at once, a request for secrecy, fees to be paid first, and no clear account of how the money is made. Any single sign, she said, was reason enough to stop, and this leaflet, she added dryly, had managed all five of them.

Joel, who was by now rather more cautious than he used to be, telephoned the man and put three plain questions to him: who stood behind the scheme, how it made its money, and where its rules could be checked. The answers were vague, impatient and finally rude, and Joel politely thanked the man for his time and ended the call. He felt as though he had passed a test that he had not known he was sitting.

Another day brought a text message that claimed to come from the bank and asked Amara to click on a link and confirm her password within the hour. She looked at it carefully, noticed the odd spelling and the sense of panic that it was trying to create, and remembered that a real bank never asks for a password in this way. She deleted the message at once and told Joel, so that he would know what to look for.

Dev rang Amara in a fluster to say that he had received an urgent call from someone who claimed to work for his bank, telling him to move his money to a safe account straight away. He had almost obeyed, but a small doubt made him hang up and call the bank on the number printed on his card, and the bank confirmed that it was a trick. Amara told him that his instinct, and his new habit of checking, had very probably saved him a small fortune.

Ivy brought the tablet to the table to show her parents a bright pop-up that offered a heap of free gems if she would only enter a code and a name. The family agreed on a simple rule for every offer that appears online, which they wrote on a card and stuck above the screen: stop, wait, and ask a grown-up. Ivy added a small drawing of a stop sign, and Noah coloured it red.

Every week, on Sunday morning, Amara sat down at the kitchen table with a mug of tea and the notebook while Joel set the timer on his phone for ten minutes. A short regular check, Aunt Wen had told them, keeps a family informed and calm, because small problems are noticed while they are still small and cheap to fix. It took no more effort than a cup of tea, and it was worth far more.

The weekly check followed a short list that Ivy had copied out in her best handwriting: the balances, the bills that were coming, the contents of the jars, and one question for the week. Nothing was hidden, nothing was judged, and nothing took longer than the tea took to cool, which was why they never skipped it. It had become less a chore than a quiet ritual that closed the weekend.

During one of those weekly checks Joel noticed a payment of nine to an online shop that none of the family had ever used, and his stomach tightened until he remembered what to do. He telephoned the bank at once, explained the matter in a calm voice, and within a few days the charge was cancelled and the money returned. Had they checked only once a year, the thief might have taken a good deal more.

Aunt Wen held up a wide kitchen scale and balanced a bag of flour against a bag of sugar to explain a simple idea. Net worth, she said, is everything you own minus everything you owe, and it is the truest measure of how a family is doing. Checking it once a year, rather than every week, shows real progress without the daily worry.

Joel wrote two columns on a clean page, headed Own and Owe, and added up each one carefully on the calculator. The big credit card had by now been paid off completely, which gave him a pleasure that he could not describe, and the family's net worth came to about four thousand. He turned the calculator round on the table and showed the figure to Amara without saying a single word, and she began to smile.

Amara fetched last year's page from the back of the notebook and laid it beside this year's, and the contrast was startling. A year earlier, the number had been about minus one thousand, which meant that the family had owed more than it owned, so the direction of change mattered even more than the figure itself. They had climbed out of a deep hole, she realised, without ever noticing each of the small steps that had carried them out.

Joel looked at the old car and a printed list of used car prices, and he wondered how to count something that would never be sold. Aunt Wen told him to count every item at what it would fetch if sold today, not at what he had paid, and to leave out dreams, wishes and the optimistic opinions of friends. An honest number, she said with a firm nod, is always worth far more than a flattering number that cannot be trusted.

Amara and Joel had always enjoyed being generous, and they had no wish to become the sort of people who counted every coin in front of a friend in need. Aunt Wen agreed that giving belongs in a healthy plan, so they added a small line for gifts and for helping others, and they filled it before any other fun spending. Planned generosity, she said, is the kind that never leaves regrets, because it comes from the heart and not from the leftovers.

When Lina's family had a hard week, Joel and Amara carried a pot of hot soup and a loaf of bread to their door, and Amara slipped in a card. The giving jar paid for the ingredients, and the visit was handled so gently that nobody felt embarrassed or small. Lina hugged Amara on the doorstep for rather longer than usual, and neither of them said much.

At the next family meeting Ivy and Noah were asked to decide where the family's yearly gift should go, and the discussion lasted nearly an hour. They studied two leaflets with enormous seriousness and finally chose a local animal shelter, partly because of a photograph of a three-legged dog. They felt very proud of the decision they had made, and the grown-ups, watching them, felt prouder still.

At the depot office, a woman from the personnel department slid a paper across the desk that described a retirement plan with a matching contribution. When an employer adds money to a plan whenever a worker pays in, she explained, that match is a bonus that is hard to beat, although the rules differ from one country and one company to another. Amara had walked past the poster on the wall for years without ever stopping to read a single word of it.

Amara circled a line on the leaflet that promised fifty from the company for every fifty that she paid in, and she took it to Aunt Wen that evening. Aunt Wen read it twice and said that such a match is an instant gain, so taking it was worth doing even before extra debt payments, though she urged Amara to read the exact terms and ask any questions. Rules vary a great deal from place to place, she said, and in a matter of money the small details always matter.

On Friday Amara signed the form at the depot office and agreed to pay in fifty a month, and the employer promised to add another fifty to the plan. She walked out into the sunshine feeling as though she had found money lying on the pavement, and she told Joel the news before she had even taken off her coat. It was, he said with a grin, quite possibly the easiest raise that either of them had ever earned in their lives.

A year after the first spending diary, Amara drove her last bus of the day into the depot at dusk and handed the house key to Joel, who was waiting at the gate. They had agreed that this evening would be an anniversary of sorts, a quiet occasion to look back over the road they had travelled. Neither of them could quite believe that twelve whole months had passed so quickly, or that so much had changed in that time.

They sat at the kitchen table and opened the old notebook, and they compared its early pages with the most recent ones, which were neat and calm. Two of the three debts had disappeared, the sofa loan was small, and the Safety account held nearly two thousand, which was almost three weeks of essential costs. The numbers were not dramatic, but taken together they described a different family from the one that had sat there a year before.

To mark the anniversary, the whole family planted a small apple tree in the shared garden behind their building, and Ivy dug the hole with the seriousness of an engineer. Noah poured water on the roots from a bucket that was almost larger than he was, while Amara and Joel pressed the soil down gently and tied the young trunk to a stake. It was a thin and rather unimpressive little thing, but, as Aunt Wen would have said, every large tree begins as a beginning.

Noah sat back on his heels beside the sapling and asked, with perfect seriousness, how long it would take to give them an apple. Aunt Wen, who had come to watch, said that it would be a few years and that it could not be hurried, any more than a savings account could. Money, she added, grows in the dark, and rewards only those who are patient enough to leave it alone.

That evening they looked back over the year, with the calendar spread out between them, and Amara said what they were all beginning to understand. No single heroic decision had transformed their finances, she said, but hundreds of ordinary small choices, repeated week after week, had slowly turned the direction of their lives. A habit that costs little and is kept for years will always beat a grand gesture that is soon dropped.

Ivy took a card and wrote five lines on it in her best handwriting, and then she stuck it to the fridge with a magnet shaped like a strawberry. Write it down, pay yourself first, wait two days, let it run on autopilot, and check every week: those were the habits that she thought had mattered most. When her parents read the list aloud, they could not think of a single thing to add.

Aunt Wen sat on a wooden chair in her old shop, which was now run by a young couple who had let her keep her seat by the window, and she smiled at the passing customers. Real wealth, she told Amara and Joel, is not what you show to the world, but what you keep and what it allows you to do. A person who has money to spare for a crisis, she said, owns something that no shop window can display.

Aunt Wen told them about a customer from her early years who had worn the same patched coat for a decade and had always counted his coins at the counter, slowly and with great care. He never bought anything grand, and some of the neighbours had pitied him, but many years later he paid for his grandchildren's school without a word to anyone. Looks, she concluded with a smile, are a very poor guide to what a person really has, or to what a person is worth.

Rosa heard about the notebook from Joel's cheerful chatter and asked him to share his method with the other bakers, who had often wondered how he had changed. On Friday morning Joel stood at her long table with a plate of warm rolls and spoke about leaks, jars and paying yourself first, and he was surprised by how many people leaned forward to listen. Two of them asked for a copy of the three columns before he had finished.

At the end of the evening Amara and Joel ticked a box on a paper that read Sofa Loan by Spring, and they looked across the room at the new thermometer on the fridge door. The red line had already climbed two thirds of the way, and when Noah coloured in the next inch, with a theatrical flourish, the whole family applauded. It was a small ceremony, but nobody who was present that evening, not even the youngest, was ever likely to forget it.

One evening Amara and Joel sat down with a fresh sheet of paper and wrote down their goals for the next twenty years. They hoped for a home with no debt, school costs paid for the children, and a comfortable later life in which neither of them would be anxious. They drew a small star on the calendar beside a date that was still many years away, and the star made the future feel like a place that could really be reached by two people walking together.

Aunt Wen helped them sort every goal into one of three circles, labelled this year, five years and twenty years, and the sorting made the whole task feel less crowded. Safety and Yearly Bills belonged in the first circle, the children's school costs in the second, and the later life they hoped to enjoy in the last. A goal that has no date, she observed with a smile, is only a wish wearing a very good costume.

Beside each goal Amara wrote one small action for the coming month, because a distant dream feels possible only when the first step is clear. For the longest goal, the step was to begin a regular investment of one hundred a month in a low-cost fund, understanding that its value could rise and fall. It was money that they would not need for many years, and they both agreed that it was a modest and sensible beginning.

A year and a half after the first spending diary, a letter arrived from the bank, and Amara read it standing in the hall with her coat still on. The Safety account now held a full month of essential costs, every debt was gone, and the new investment account had its first small balance, which she studied with delighted disbelief. She laughed aloud, and Joel came running from the kitchen to see what had happened.

Amara noticed one evening that she no longer lay awake at night calculating what might go wrong, because her savings stood quietly behind her like a solid wall. The numbers had grown slowly, but the feeling of security had arrived much faster than she had expected. Money, she thought, is only a tool, and yet it can give a person the most valuable thing of all, which is a little peace.

Joel drew a small bakery on a paper napkin, with a striped awning, a wooden counter and a gleaming oven, and he looked at it for a long time. Rather than rush into a risky loan, he gave the dream a name, the Oven Fund, and a plan to test it slowly by selling at the market and by saving a little for it each month. A dream, he had learned over the past eighteen months, is always much safer and far more likely to come true when it has a jar.

At school, Ivy placed three small jars on her desk during the break and explained to a classmate how Save, Spend and Share worked, with the confidence of a professor. The friend listened with wide eyes and then asked where she could buy jars like those, and by the end of the week, three more children had made labels. Good habits, it turned out, can spread among friends as quietly and as quickly as any rumour in a school playground.

Aunt Wen took her old green ledger from the shelf, dusted its cover with her sleeve and placed it into Amara's hands, saying that it belonged to her now. The plan, she said, needs only to be kept up, and not to be made perfect, because the families who succeed are not those who never slip but those who always begin again. Amara held the heavy old book against her chest for a long moment and found that she could not speak.

In spring the thin branches of the little apple tree, which had seemed so unimpressive a year before, opened into a cloud of white blossom that hummed with bees. Noah counted every flower twice, wrote the number in the notebook in large and slightly crooked figures, and insisted that the whole family come outside to admire it. Even Aunt Wen, who had seen a great many springs, stood quite still with her hand over her mouth.

Small savings, made patiently and kept up for many years, can quietly build a very large future for an ordinary family. This book is general information and not financial advice, and every household has its own circumstances, so anyone with a particular question should consult a qualified adviser. Amara, Joel and the children looked at their little tree and understood that the best time to begin had been yesterday, and the second best was now.
